name: Schein-Aichelburg Wormhole Between Charged Shells
description: A static, axially symmetric wormhole whose two mouths open into the same universe, built by Friedrich Schein and Peter Christian Aichelburg in 1996 from two charged spheres held apart by their electric repulsion. Outside the spheres is the Majumdar-Papapetrou field, inside them one Reissner-Nordström black hole, and the shells of charged matter on the spheres can satisfy all the energy conditions. A traveller crosses the black hole from one mouth to the other in one direction only, and every point outside lies on a closed timelike curve.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: At the Institute for Theoretical Physics of the University of Vienna, Friedrich Schein and Peter Christian Aichelburg built a wormhole in 1996 whose two mouths open into the same universe [schein1996]. Two charged spheres stay at rest in it, their electric repulsion balancing their gravitational attraction, and a traveller who falls into one of them comes out of the other [schein1996]. They made it from two exact solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell equations, the static field of charged bodies in equilibrium that Sudhansu Datta Majumdar and Achilles Papapetrou found in 1947 and the Reissner-Nordström black hole [schein1996, majumdar1947, papapetrou1947, reissner1916, nordstrom1918]. A wormhole whose mouths share one universe can have at most an axial symmetry, here about the line through the two spheres [schein1996, aichelburg1998]. The matter on the spheres can obey all the energy conditions, and every point outside them lies on a closed timelike curve [schein1996, aichelburg1998]. Schein, Aichelburg, and Werner Israel had held two uncharged particles apart earlier that year with strings running to infinity, and their wormhole needed matter of negative energy density on its mouths [schein1996string].¶Majumdar and Papapetrou's metric, $ds^2 = -c^2dT^2/V^2 + V^2(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$, solves the Einstein-Maxwell equations wherever $V$ solves Laplace's equation in the flat coordinates $x$, $y$, and $z$ [schein1996, aichelburg1998]. Schein and Aichelburg cut out of that spacetime the insides of two spheres of radius $R$ centred at $z = \pm d_1$, and asked for $V$ to take one value on both, $V_0 = 1 + m_1/R$ [schein1996]. That is the problem of the electric potential outside two charged metal spheres [schein1996]. They solved it with a series of image charges $m_n$ on the axis at $z = \pm d_n$, following Richard Lindquist, who had used the method of inversion images in 1963 for time symmetric initial data on manifolds with Einstein-Rosen bridges [schein1996, lindquist1963]. In bispherical coordinates $\mu$, $\eta$, and $\phi$ the two spheres are the surfaces $\mu = \pm\mu_0$ [schein1996]. When the spheres are far apart, the field around them is that of two particles whose mass and charge are both $m_1$ [schein1996, aichelburg1998].¶Inside the spheres sits a Reissner-Nordström black hole of mass $m$ and charge $q$, with $|q| \le m$, cut at the radius $r = RV_0$ in two of its outer regions, one in the causal future of the other [schein1996]. Each cut is glued to one sphere at equal angles and equal proper times, so the two sides agree on the geometry of the seam, $ds^2 = -c^2d\tau^2 + R^2V_0^2\,d\Omega^2$, and each seam holds a thin shell of charged matter [schein1996]. The surface energy density of each shell is set by the jump in extrinsic curvature across it, through the junction conditions of Israel [israel1966, schein1996]. Schein and Aichelburg showed that for $R/d_1 \le 1/3$ the energy density is positive all over both shells once $m$ and $|q|$ are small enough [schein1996]. Aichelburg and Schein extended that in 1998, with the boundary point lemma and the maximum principles of elliptic equations, to any two spheres that do not touch, $R < d_1$, where for small enough $m$ and $|q|$ the shells satisfy all the energy conditions [aichelburg1998]. On each shell the energy density changes with the angle, and the two tangential pressures are equal and constant [aichelburg1998].¶A traveller passes from one shell to the other through the black hole, across its horizons and in one direction only [aichelburg1998, smirnov2016]. Aichelburg and Schein put the throat on a spacelike slice half way through the Reissner-Nordström wormhole, with one mouth in the future of the other [aichelburg1998]. Every point of one shell can be reached by a causal curve through the black hole from every point of the other, so a traveller can come out arbitrarily far in the past and meet a "former self" [schein1996, aichelburg1998]. Every event outside the shells lies on a closed causal curve, which makes the wormhole, in their words, an "eternal" time machine [aichelburg1998, schein1996]. The gluing leaves a constant shift of time free, which can be set so that observers falling freely along the axis come back to their starting point in space and time [schein1996].¶John Friedman, Kristin Schleich, and Donald Witt proved in 1993 that in a globally hyperbolic, asymptotically flat spacetime obeying the averaged null energy condition, every causal curve from past to future null infinity can be deformed into a topologically trivial one [friedman1993]. Aichelburg and Schein pointed out that their spacetime is not globally hyperbolic [aichelburg1998]. Gregory Galloway and Eric Woolgar replaced global hyperbolicity in 1997 by cosmic censorship and a condition at spatial infinity they called "$i^0$-avoidance", and proved under those assumptions and the focusing of null geodesics that the domain of outer communications is simply connected [galloway1997]. Schein and Aichelburg's wormhole satisfies the energy conditions and violates $i^0$-avoidance, since "through every point of the asymptotic region there is a closed timelike curve" [galloway1997]. Galloway and Woolgar took it, together with a second example, as evidence that a condition of that kind cannot be dispensed with entirely [galloway1997]. Gérard Clément called it a static Wheeler-Misner wormhole, one with a single region at spatial infinity, which is "traversable only one way" [clement1997].¶John Moffat adapted the construction in 2015 to MOG, a modified gravity whose vector field couples to a charge proportional to mass [moffat2015]. Alexey Smirnov built a cosmological version in 2016, with the expanding universe of David Kastor and Jennie Traschen's charged black holes outside the shells and a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole inside [smirnov2016, kastor1993]. Its shells have to be dust, with no pressure, and they expand with the universe [smirnov2016]. Smirnov called the static wormhole the "Aichelburg-Schein timehole", one a traveller can cross only one way, through horizons [smirnov2016]. The cosmological timehole inherits the instability of the Cauchy horizon of its black hole, which Schein and Aichelburg had noted for the static wormhole [smirnov2016, schein1996]. Closed causal curves form there if the shells are close enough together, and a particle horizon that later grows between the shells breaks those curves, so that time machine is not eternal [smirnov2016].

related.text: The outside of the shells, Majumdar and Papapetrou's field of two charged bodies at rest, with $V$ held at one value on both spheres by a series of image charges [schein1996].
The inside of the shells, one Reissner-Nordström black hole cut at the radius $r = RV_0$ in two of its outer regions, one in the future of the other [schein1996].

A wormhole made into a time machine by moving one mouth, with closed timelike curves only beyond a Cauchy horizon. Outside the two charged shells closed timelike curves pass through every event, for all time [aichelburg1998].

Another wormhole held open by thin shells, with one shell of negative energy density joining two universes. The two charged shells join one universe to itself and can obey the energy conditions [schein1996].
A single shell of charged dust with Reissner and Nordström's field outside. The two charged shells hold that field between them, and a traveller crosses it from one shell to the other [schein1996].
The shell of dust that Werner Israel solved with the junction conditions in 1966. The same conditions set the energy density of the two charged shells [israel1966, schein1996].

Charged black holes in an expanding universe. Alexey Smirnov put two charged shells into it in 2016, with a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole between them, and got a cosmological version of this wormhole [smirnov2016].

Initial data for black holes at rest. Richard Lindquist found such data for charged bridges with inversion images in 1963, the method behind the potential outside the two charged spheres [lindquist1963, schein1996].

parameters.description: Dimensionless potential, $V = 1 + \sum_{n \geq 1} m_n\left(|\mathbf{x} - d_n\hat{\mathbf{z}}|^{-1} + |\mathbf{x} + d_n\hat{\mathbf{z}}|^{-1}\right)$ over the image charges $m_n = (-1)^{n+1}m_1\sinh\mu_0/\sinh n\mu_0$, harmonic outside the spheres, $1 + m_1/R$ on both, and 1 at infinity; the components hold for any $V$, harmonic or not
Radius of each sphere, a length, with $R < d_1$

Distance of each sphere's centre from the origin, a length; the images of the potential sit at $d_n = a\coth n\mu_0$ for integer $n \geq 1$, with $a = \sqrt{d_1^2 - R^2}$ and $\mu_0 = \operatorname{arccosh}(d_1/R)$
Mass parameter of each sphere, $m_1 = GM_1/c^2$, a length; when the spheres are far apart each has the mass $M_1$ and a charge $Q_1$ with $GQ_1^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4) = m_1^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, x, y, z)$ outside the spheres, with $T$ having dimensions of time, $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths, $\mathbf{x} = (x, y, z)$, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ the unit vector along the axis through the two centres. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.
